planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring into average, well-drained soil in full sun; the apothecary rose is one of the oldest roses in continuous cultivation, historically grown for medicinal and culinary petal use.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; the apothecary rose is a compact, suckering, semi-double, deep pink to crimson rose grown in European monastery and apothecary gardens for centuries for its intensely fragrant petals, historically dried for medicinal preparations, potpourri, and rosewater, and famous as the heraldic Red Rose of Lancaster. It blooms once in late spring in a heavy, richly perfumed flush, followed by small orange-red hips that add fall interest if left unpruned. Own-root plants sucker readily to form a dense thicket over time, which can be an asset for an informal hedge or a nuisance in a tightly maintained border, so plan its placement with that spreading habit in mind. It is remarkably disease-resistant and cold-hardy compared to modern hybrid roses, needing only routine deadwood removal after its single bloom flush rather than the intensive spraying and pruning modern roses often require.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown shrubs in late winter to early spring into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; damask rose is the classic perfume rose grown commercially in Bulgaria, Turkey, and Iran for attar of roses and rosewater distillation.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; damask rose is an ancient hybrid species prized above nearly any other rose for the depth and quality of its fragrance, the source of true attar of roses and rosewater produced commercially in the valleys of Bulgaria, Turkey, and Iran. Loosely double, pink to light red flowers open over a generous spring flush, and some strains rebloom lightly in fall, though the once-blooming forms remain the most commonly grown for fragrance and hip production. Petals are traditionally hand-harvested at dawn, when essential oil content peaks, for distillation, drying, or use in culinary rosewater and preserves. It grows into a tall, somewhat lax, arching shrub that benefits from light support or informal training, and like other old garden roses, it is generally more disease-resistant and needs less routine spraying than modern hybrid tea roses.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown shrubs in late winter to early spring into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; cabbage rose has a lax, arching habit and benefits from support or informal training against a fence or trellis.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; cabbage rose is a complex old hybrid renowned for its extremely full, densely packed, globular flowers with dozens of tightly overlapping petals arranged in the swirling, layered form that made it the favorite subject of Dutch and French flower painters for centuries, most famously Pierre-Joseph Redouté. Its rich, classic old-rose fragrance is nearly as celebrated as its form, and the petals are used in the same rosewater and rose-oil traditions as damask rose, particularly in the historic Provence perfume industry that gave the plant one of its common names. Flowering occurs in a single generous flush in late spring, on a lax, somewhat floppy shrub that looks best trained loosely against a support or allowed to arch naturally among other cottage garden plants. Prune lightly right after flowering to shape, since it blooms on old wood and heavy dormant-season pruning removes the coming season's flowers.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown shrubs in late winter to early spring into well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun; Austrian copper rose is exceptionally cold hardy and is the historic source of true yellow and orange coloring in modern rose breeding.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun; Austrian copper rose is a tough, exceptionally cold-hardy species rose bearing single, brilliant orange-red flowers with a bright yellow reverse that gives an unusual two-toned, flame-like effect in the garden, especially striking en masse or against dark foliage. It blooms in a single, intense flush in late spring and was historically the key source of true yellow pigment introduced into modern rose breeding lines, since most older roses could produce only white, pink, or red tones. The species carries a distinctive, somewhat unpleasant scent noted in its species name (foetida means foul-smelling in Latin), most noticeable up close rather than at a distance. It tolerates poor, dry soil and harsh winter cold better than most other old garden roses, making it a good choice for a tough, low-input hedge or specimen in a cold, challenging site, requiring only removal of dead wood after its single spring bloom.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown shrubs in spring into average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade with a fence, arbor, or large shrub to lean on; musk rose is a vigorous, rambling species less cold-hardy than most European old garden roses.

directions: Plant against a fence, arbor, or large shrub for support in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; musk rose is a vigorous, semi-climbing to rambling species rose with clusters of small, single to semi-double, creamy white flowers carrying a distinctive sweet musk fragrance most pronounced in the evening, when it was traditionally prized in cottage and cutting gardens. Unlike most once-blooming old garden roses, it flowers later in the season, from midsummer into fall, extending the old-rose bloom season after spring-flowering gallicas, damasks, and centifolias have finished. It is an important ancestor of the modern hybrid musk and Noisette rose classes, contributing both fragrance and repeat or late bloom to its descendants. Being somewhat less cold-hardy and more vigorous than European gallica-type roses, give it a warm, sheltered site with room to ramble, and prune after flowering to control size on the sprawling, long canes.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring into humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; gold fountains sedge holds its bright variegated color best out of direct hot afternoon sun.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; gold fountains sedge forms a neat, arching mound of slender leaves edged in bright gold, the variegation showing strongest in the cultivar 'Kaga-nishiki' widely sold under this common name. Its fine, fountain-like texture and bright color brighten shaded plantings without the maintenance and disease concerns of many flowering shade perennials, holding good color from spring through fall in climates with humid summers. Inconspicuous flower spikes appear in spring but are incidental to the foliage display that is the plant's main ornamental feature. It combines well at the front of a shade border with hostas, ferns, and heucheras, providing a fine-textured, brightly colored contrast to their broader leaves, and it divides easily every few years in spring if a planting needs to be expanded or rejuvenated.
